message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated that the game has a “Shannon number” of about  

\[
10^{43}
\]

possible positions.  More recent research, which takes into account all the rules of chess (castling rights, en‑passant, pawn promotion, etc.) and counts only *legal* positions, puts the figure in the range of

\[
10^{45}\text{–}10^{46}
\]

(roughly 1 × 10^45 to 3 × 10^45).  If you include *illegal* arrangements as well, the count climbs to roughly \(10^{47}\).

So, in short, there are on the order of **10^45** possible legal arrangements of pieces on a chessboard.
